## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Vammika Sutta* ("The Ant-Hill", MN 23) is the twenty-third discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The narrative centers on an enigmatic riddle presented by a deity to the monk Kumārakassapa regarding an ant-hill that smokes by night and blazes by day [SuttaCentral; Underwood 1973]. In the vision, an anonymous brahman urges Kumārakassapa, addressed as "wise one" (*sumedha*), to take up a knife or blade (*sattha*) and dig; Kumārakassapa subsequently approaches the Buddha, who decodes the symbolic riddle [Underwood 1973; Beckwith; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995].
In the Buddha's exposition, the ant-hill represents the human body [Humphreys 1956]. Its smoking by night and blazing by day illustrate the everyday mind pondering and planning (*anuvitakketvā anuvicāretvā*) during the night before executing actions through body, speech, and mind during the day [Polak 2011]. The knife used to dig represents wisdom or discernment (*paññā*), a metaphor reflected in the traditional phrase *paññā-sattha* [Underwood 1973; Denwood & Piatigorsky 1983]. Through this blade of wisdom, Kumārakassapa digs out and discards successive obstacles: ignorance (*avijjā*), anger (*kodha*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇa*), the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), and desire and lust (*nandirāga*) [Underwood 1973]. At the bottom of the mound, a serpent (*nāga*) is reached, which the Buddha reveals to symbolize an arahant monk who has completely destroyed the fluxes or cankers (*āsava*) and is worthy of veneration [Beckwith]. Later commentarial tradition (*Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*) on the sutta also incorporates an account of the relics and caitya of Buddha Kassapa [Skilling].
SuttaCentral records full parallels in the Chinese Āgamas: *Ekottarika-āgama* discourse EĀ 39.9, *Saṁyuktāgama* discourses SĀ 1079 and SĀ² 18 (T 100.18), as well as an independent translation in Taishō 95 [SuttaCentral; Dhammadinna 2013]. DharmaNexus aligns the text with both the *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100) and the *Za ahan jing* (T 99)—confirming the Āgama parallels—and notes correspondences with the Tibetan *Udānavargavivaraṇa* (D 4100) and T 53 [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus detects 685 shared reuse passages across 76 texts, with the largest volume of matches occurring in the *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6), *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Devatā Saṁyutta* (SN 1), and *Sattakanipāta* (AN 7) [DharmaNexus].
